A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ComfyBench and ComfyAgent study. Their main text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and comparable, including the retained prompt templates and worked trajectory despite reflow and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original ComfyBench evaluations, representation and architecture ablations, human–GPT-4o agreement measurements, and generated examples.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds token consumption, generation-quality comparisons, additional multi-agent comparisons, and expanded human-validation results.

M1.justification: The reversible code/workflow representation and Memory, Planner, and Actions framework remain unchanged. The planning, combination, adaptation, retrieval, and refinement procedures and appendix prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: The 200-task image/video benchmark and its difficulty categories remain unchanged. However, validator coverage expands from ComfyAgent-completed tasks to include human-constructed outputs for 20 tasks ComfyAgent did not complete, introducing another source of outputs into the human–VLM comparison.

E2.justification: v3 substantially broadens the evaluated comparator families: new Table 6 compares against DALL-E 3 and InstructPix2Pix, while new Table 7 compares against CAMEL and Multi-agent Debate (MAD). The original Table 2 comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The human study expands from 50 questions and 400 human judgments to 70 questions and 560 judgments, including 20 manually constructed outputs. v3 also adds HPSv2/Aesthetic scoring on available image outputs and average token consumption. The main benchmark's pass/resolve evaluation protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds a targeted examination of generated-image quality beyond workflow execution and instruction satisfaction. The human–VLM reliability analysis is also extended. The representation and component-removal ablations, illustrative cases, and worked trajectory remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions average eight human judgments and eight GPT-4o responses per question and report the same Kendall, Pearson, and Spearman statistics with p-values. The larger question set and changed statistical values do not introduce a different repetition or uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial result categories: token costs, image-quality scores, and CAMEL/MAD comparisons. Examples include 14.96k tokens for GPT-4o ComfyAgent and creative-task resolve rates of 0%, 2.5%, and 15% for CAMEL, MAD, and ComfyAgent. Table 1's Pearson correlation changes from 0.791 to 0.764 on the expanded validation sample. Existing benchmark pass/resolve and ablation scores are unchanged.

T1.justification: The DAG/workflow description and pass/resolve definitions are retained. The added quality metrics are named without new mathematical definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The benchmark and code-based multi-agent contributions, comparable performance to o1-preview, and 15% creative-task resolution remain the central claims. The revised contribution bullet emphasizes multi-agent design, but the code-representation advantage remains asserted and supported by the retained ablation.

C2.justification: Appendix G newly interprets the quality scores as showing generation quality similar to single-model methods. Section 5.3 removes the explicit interpretation of o1-preview's performance as showcasing strong reasoning. The substantive open-loop and fine-tuning limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix F discloses agent temperature 1.0, evaluator temperature 0, and other parameters retained at model defaults; these are disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to earlier settings. v3 also supplies code and project-site links and reports video examples as available rather than forthcoming.

R1.justification: v3 adds Liang et al.'s multi-agent debate reference and removes the AutoGPT and SGLang references. The related-work narrative and overall novelty positioning remain largely unchanged, while the new comparisons provide more direct positioning against existing methods.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized introduction and conclusion edits, corrects wording, updates affiliations, and adds acknowledgments. It moves the supplementary examples discussion earlier and adds Sections F–H, while retaining the main section structure and most prose.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains a token-cost column, two comparison tables are added, and the correlation heatmap is updated. The questionnaire figure moves, existing appendix tables are renumbered, and trajectory page breaks improve. Existing diagrams and example images are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 improves transparency and empirical support through token-cost reporting, inference parameters, access information, additional comparators, and broader human validation. These are useful additions to an otherwise stable method and benchmark. The gains remain limited because the new comparisons have sparse setup descriptions and the quality scores use each method's available outputs without establishing matched evaluation subsets.
